title: John 12:20–36
context: Some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. A grain of wheat must die to bear much fruit, and whoever loves his life loses it. Jesus’ soul is troubled, but he will not ask to be saved from this hour; he came for it. A voice from heaven answers his prayer to glorify the Father’s name. Now is the judgment of this world and the casting out of its ruler, and when he is lifted up, Jesus will draw all people to himself. He urges the crowd to believe in the light while they have it. Verse 32 is a key text in the debate over the Father’s drawing in 6:44.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic comment on the grain of wheat and the lifted Son who draws, from both sides of the debate.
voices.note: Quotations abridged; wording follows standard English editions of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Lifted up from the earth—This is a Hebraism which signifies dying. Death in general is all that is usually imported.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 12:32)

reformed.quote: Christ, being lifted up on the cross, shall gather all men to himself, in order that he may raise them from earth to heaven. The cross will be, as it were, a chariot, by which he shall raise all men, along with himself, to his Father.

verses.text: Now there were certain Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast.
verses.arminianNotes: Some Greeks were among those who went up to worship. Arminian readers see Gentiles seeking Jesus as a sign that the gospel is for all nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the arrival of the Greeks as the sign that Christ’s hour, when he will gather the nations, has come.

verses.text: Therefore, these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, “Sir, we want to see Jesus.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.” Arminian readers see genuine seeking, which grace has awakened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Gentiles drawn to Christ, the beginning of the gathering of the other sheep (10:16).

verses.text: Philip came and told Andrew, and in turn, Andrew came with Philip, and they told Jesus.
verses.arminianNotes: Philip told Andrew, and they told Jesus. Arminian readers see the disciples bringing seekers to Jesus.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the role of human messengers in bringing people to Christ.

verses.text: Jesus answered them, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.
verses.arminianNotes: The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Arminian readers see the cross as the moment that opens salvation to the world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the hour appointed by the Father now arriving.

verses.text: Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
verses.arminianNotes: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Arminian readers see Christ’s death producing a great harvest available to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s death certainly producing fruit, the people he came to save.

verses.text: He who loves his life will lose it. He who hates his life in this world will keep it to eternal life.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life. Arminian readers see a real choice set before every disciple.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see self-denial as the mark of those who belong to Christ.

verses.text: If anyone serves me, let him follow me. Where I am, there my servant will also be. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.
verses.arminianNotes: If anyone serves me, he must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also. Arminian readers see the call to follow as ongoing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the promise that Christ’s servants will be with him.

verses.text: “Now my soul is troubled. What shall I say? ‘Father, save me from this time’? But I came to this time for this cause.
verses.arminianNotes: Now is my soul troubled. Shall I say, Father, save me from this hour? No, for this purpose I have come. Arminian readers see Christ’s real human anguish and free submission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s true humanity and his obedience to the Father’s eternal plan.

verses.text: Father, glorify your name!” Then a voice came out of the sky, saying, “I have both glorified it and will glorify it again.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Father, glorify your name.” A voice came: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” Arminian readers see the Father affirming the Son’s mission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s glory as the final purpose of redemption.

verses.text: Therefore the multitude who stood by and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd said it had thundered; others said an angel had spoken. Arminian readers see varied responses to the same revelation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that people need spiritual sight to perceive God’s voice.

verses.text: Jesus answered, “This voice hasn’t come for my sake, but for your sakes.
verses.arminianNotes: This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Arminian readers see God giving evidence to help people believe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s testimony given for the sake of his people.

verses.text: Now is the judgment of this world. Now the prince of this world will be cast out.
verses.arminianNotes: Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out. Arminian readers see the cross defeating Satan for the whole world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the cross as the decisive victory over Satan, freeing Christ’s people from his power.

verses.text: And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”
verses.arminianNotes:
And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself. Arminian readers see this as the key to 6:44. The Father’s drawing reaches all people through the cross, enabling everyone to respond.

They see “all people” as every person without exception.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the context of the Greeks (v20) and read “all people” as all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews. They see the drawing as effectual, as in 6:44.

They hold that this is consistent with effectual grace for the elect from every nation.
verses.keyContrast: Both see the cross drawing people to Christ. Arminian readers see “all people” as everyone without exception, with a drawing that can be resisted. Reformed readers see it as all kinds of people, prompted by the Greeks’ arrival, and the drawing as effectual for those drawn.

verses.text: But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die.
verses.arminianNotes: He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die. Arminian readers see the lifting up as the cross.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s death foreknown and appointed.

verses.text: The multitude answered him, “We have heard out of the law that the Christ remains forever. How do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? Who is this Son of Man?”
verses.arminianNotes: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever.” Arminian readers see the crowd’s confusion about a suffering Messiah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inability of natural understanding to grasp the cross.

verses.text: Jesus therefore said to them, “Yet a little while the light is with you. Walk while you have the light, that darkness doesn’t overtake you. He who walks in the darkness doesn’t know where he is going.
verses.arminianNotes: The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light. Arminian readers see an urgent call to respond before the opportunity passes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the seriousness of the present moment of grace.

verses.text: While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become children of light.” Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them.
verses.arminianNotes: While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light. Arminian readers see a genuine invitation to every hearer to believe and become God’s children.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command to believe as sincere, addressed to all, and used by God to call his people.
